718 Boxster / Cayman Telemetry for Motorsport Lap Timers
Choosing Your Telemetry Path & Driver Type

Contributed by @Cali_Chuck, @WebKris, @SJFehr, @artem981 & @phil_beRevised Sep 23, 2026

This page is a tutorial companion to the Master CAN & OBD Signal List for Base (2.0L) and S/GTS (2.5L).

Choosing a Telemetry Path – Which Driver Are You?

The sheer number of telemetry signals available on a 718 combined with the variety of possible methods of obtaining them can make it hard to know where to start.

To clarify the valid choices and help with your decision making, here is an intentionally oversimplified set of four different telemetry "paths." You can use this framework to quickly down select the options that apply to your particular and unique combination of vehicle features, driving experience, comfort with vehicle modification and data objectives.

Obviously this framework won't apply to every driver, for instance there are plenty of "expert / racer" drivers who employ the Garmin catalyst device as their primary "coach" and would happily add an OBD connector to get "core" driver telemetry were Garmin to ever offer that capability. This chart also does not take into account the plethora of third party aftermarket sensors for things like real time tire temperature and pressure sensing.

Here are the key takeaways from this chart:

  • Drivers of every skill level can benefit from telemetry!
  • This is especially true for novice drivers who have access to data "coaches" at their events. Drivers can progress their skills very quickly with just 2-3 "core" data signals (accelerator & brake pedals plus vehicle speed).
  • The bulk of "core" driver telemetry can be obtained without any car modification by simply adding a Bluetooth OBD dongle that is compatible with the lap timer program you are using. There are multiple dongle options but a lot of us use the products from OBDLink that connect wirelessly to a phone using Bluetooth.
  • There are two different kinds of signals on the OBD port – OBD "Basic" (or OBD-B) and OBD "Extended" (or OBD-E). The two types are explained below as well as on the Master CAN & OBD Signal List.
  • The only reason to access a CAN bus is to obtain "pro" level driver and engine telemetry. The main difference between "pro" and "core" levels is data frequency – OBD doesn't come very fast, and slows down quickly the more data you request. CAN is up to 50X faster than OBD with no ceiling on requests.
  • "Deep" engine Telemetry exists on 718 but is only of practical use to a very narrow set of enthusiasts who are actively modifying their engines, playing with fuel types and/or modifying air/fuel mixtures. Even most expert / racer drivers do not require the bulk of the vast telemetry that is available from a modern ECU.

With all this in mind, let us consider each of the four telemetry paths in turn, including the typical attributes of each type of driver and the specific data signals / channels of interest that are available to each one.

Driver #1 – Core Driver Telemetry for Lap Timer Apps

This category is for the motorsport driver that just wants the basic car telemetry captured by a lap timer for their own analysis or working with a data coach. Certainly this description applies to novice track or autocross drivers but could also apply to more advanced drivers focusing on just a limited set of metrics for training. This category also applies to private coaches who temporarily install their own Race Navigator, VBox or Aim Solo type hardware in a student's car and wish to plug an OBD dongle in to get core telemetry.

All this driver needs is a basic OBDLink MX+ style device. An external GPS like a RaceBox or similar product is highly recommended given the inherent inaccuracy of phone GPS and IMU sensors at track speeds – though this remains an optional choice for any driver not accessing CAN bus data. A typical channel set for Driver #1 contains just five signals (gear and brake pressure require the lap timer app to support issuing OBD-E PID requests, which RaceChrono does):

Signal NameOBD BasicOBD Extended – Flat 4
Accelerator pedal position✓✓
Brake pressure✗✓
Gear✗PDK - ✓6MT - tbd
Engine RPM✓✓
Vehicle speed✓✓

"OBD Basic" is sometimes called “Mode $01” and is the "standard" OBD query most people are familiar with. ODB-B signals are international standards that are common across all car manufacturers and models. On the Continental ECU in the 718 flat four engine there are 32 supported Protocol IDs ("PIDs"). Highly desirable signals like current gear and brake pressure are NOT available via OBD-B.

"OBD Extended (OBD-E)" Mode $22 is a manufacturer-specific and vehicle/ECU-specific set of signals that piggybacks a different protocol called UDS over the very same OBD port. This is what PIWIS / Autel / ThinkDiag / etc. use to query your engine, change codes, etc. Current Gear and brake pressure ARE available via OBD-E on flat-four Continental ECUs as well as flat-six Bosch ECUs prior to the 2025 model year.

Almost any piece of data you could think of needing is available via OBD-E, the problem is speed. OBD is transaction based — with every single inquiry for every signal having to be requested one at a time, then having to wait for each response, and repeat over and over in perpetuity. Beyond 10-15 signals OBD and OBD-E can become unusable. For the 5 "core" driver channels, a typical OBD update rate is roughly 7-10 times per second per signal.

Driver #2 – Core Driver + Basic Engine Telemetry

In addition to the 5 core signals above, Driver #2 wants to keep an eye on engine health using via a simple OBD connection. A key use case for adding a basic set of engine metrics is to understand the "normal" baseline values on your vehicle for things like key temperatures and pressures to spot problems before they become failures or codes. Another common use for such data is to be able to work backwards to possible root cause after a car throws a code on the track to help diagnose/debug a problem.

The following 6 signals apply to both turbo and NA engines and can be added to the "core" list above – not all of these are required or necessary, feel free to season to taste:

Signal NameOBD BasicOBD Extended – Flat 4
Coolant temp✓tbd
Engine oil temp✓✓
Manifold pressure (actual)✓✓
Throttle plate position (actual)✓✓
Throttle plate position (commanded)✓✓
Fuel rail pressure✓✓

Turbocharged flat-four vehicle owners should consider adding these four signals:

Signal NameOBD BasicOBD Extended – Flat 4
Exhaust gas temp✗✓
Intake air temp✓✓
Turbo boost pressure (actual)✗✓
Turbo boost pressure (commanded)✗✓

With all 5 "core" plus 10 "basic engine" channels, you will quickly discover how fast OBD slows down. A typical update rate for a driver requesting all 15 channels is no better than 1 once per second per channel. At this point the OBD port is exhausted – adding more channels will just degrade data quality. Pruning the list to just what you truly need will visibly improve the update rate.

Driver #3 – Expert Driver Needing High-Frequency Data for Coaching

Expert drivers / racers typically want the highest update rate possible in order to study the effects of their tiniest driving inputs on a millisecond-by-millisecond basis.

At this point CAN tapping becomes mandatory because of the OBD speed limit. In the best case, pulling 5-6 OBD channels at ~10 times per second each works out to an update interval of 100 milliseconds. But inside the engine and at the tires things are changing on timescales of 1 to 10 milliseconds. A 718 CAN bus will update brake pressure, engine RPM and other metrics as often as every 1-2 milliseconds. So Driver #3 doesn't really have a choice about switching from OBD to CAN.

There are six primary CAN buses on a 718 which are interconnected through a Gateway located under the dashboard. There are several diagrams later on below to help visualize this. The “Drive CAN” is strongly preferred, but the “Chassis CAN” is a good alternative (at the cost of some channels not being available – these are identified in the interactive signal tables) if the specific vehicle lacks an accessible Drive CAN. Here's a typical channel set for such a user. A high-precision external GPS like a RaceBox is also mandatory in order to accurately geo-locate CAN telemetry at millisecond update rates. There is no point in tapping into a CAN bus if the data produced is geotagged to the wrong track location.

Signal NameDrive CAN
Accelerator pedal position✓
Brake pressure✓
Current gearPDK - ✓6MT - ✓
Engine RPM (raw or smoothed)✓
Engine oil pressure✓
Engine oil temperature✓
Coolant temperature✓
PDK gearbox temperature✓

Vehicle speed (raw or smoothed)✓
Fuel level✓
Brake light status✓

Ambient temp✓
Wheel speed (FL / FR / RL / RR)✓ ✓ ✓ ✓

CAN fully replaces OBD for this type of driver / telemetry path. The OBD port is left free. Not only is CAN data up to 50X faster than OBD, but in general it is more accurate. Porsche "smooths" a number of data channels sent over the OBD port, as well as artificially truncates some data fields. CAN data is ultra-accurate because it's what the engine uses to make realtime decisions. A high level overview of CAN bus access can be found below.

Driver #4 – Engine Modder / Tuner Playing with Fuel, Airflow, Cylinder Timing and more

This driver is actively modifying the engine guts through custom intakes, turbos, valves, cylinders, custom cams, water/meth injection, fuel pumps, extra radiators, or whatever. S/he is also almost certainly running a pro tune and periodically sending data logs off somewhere for analysis & map adjustments.

This user wants everything that Driver #3 has, plus as much of a realtime X-ray of the engine as is possible to obtain.

A simultaneous combination of CAN and OBD modes is required to meet the needs of Driver #4 because while CAN is far richer than Basic OBD, on 718s it does not have a number of very desirable fields for anyone doing engine tuning. For example, turbo boost (actual) is available over CAN but the commanded boost (set point) is only on OBD-E. And most fuel / combustion signals are not available via CAN but only via OBD-B / OBD-E. This in turn requires two OBDLink type devices – one configured for OBD and one for CAN – which RaceChrono does support. One of us (@Cali_Chuck) uses both CAN and OBD-E simultaneously in exactly this way with two OBDLink MX+ sending telemetry to RaceChrono. RaceChrono supports three or more OBDLink devices operating concurrently.

Remember the OBD speed limit now applies again since we are using both CAN and OBD at the same time for different signals. It pays to choose the 10 or at most 12 signals that are most important to your use case. Do not attempt to capture every single one of these channels via OBD-B or OBD-E.

Driver #4 with a Cobb ECU tune may have to choose between have a Cobb Datalogger on the OBD port, or putting an OBDLink device on it. The advantage of going with OBD-B / OBD-E is that the resulting telemetry is both (1) time synchronized with the rest of the data stream; and (2) properly geotagged to the exact track location. The disadvantage is that Cobb has some data channels that do not exist – or at least no one has yet discovered – on OBD or CAN.

Despite what some people claim – it is NOT POSSIBLE to run two active devices simultaneously on the car's OBD port. OBD ports are engineered to have a single active device connected to them. Amazon does indeed sell "OBD splitters" but they are intended for the situation where the second OBD device is 100% "passive" and never transmits. Not only that, but ECUs themselves are not designed to handle overlapping OBD requests from multiple devices. In other words, an ECU working on a request from OBD device #1 ignores inbound requests from OBD device #2 because it is not currently listening. This behavior can be easily seen by study OBD packet traces.

Decision Tree for CAN Bus Access

The biggest factor in the decision to jump from OBD to CAN is deciding where and how to obtain access to a CAN bus. This decision is further complicated in turn by the multiplicity of vehicle configurations – principally 6MT vs. PDK and whether the Soundaktor is present or deleted. This diagram shows a basic decision tree to help aspiring CAN "tappers" to decide how to approach the challenge:

  • Generally tapping a single CAN bus is all that is required. Capturing multiple CANs is possible but outside the scope of this tutorial.
  • PDK owners should plan to access the Drive CAN because there are up to 4 different places around the vehicle to reach it that appeal to a range of wiring skill levels.
  • 6MT owners only have access to the Drive CAN from the CAN gateway under the dash. Unless they are comfortable modifying wiring in this area, the only alternative is to tap the Chassis CAN in the right rear of the vehicle where it meets the EPB controller.
  • Once you've chosen the access location, the final decision you must make is how to tap in. There are two methods.
    • "Pin split & breakout" avoids any physical penetration of CAN wiring, so it can be less risky. However, this requires you to construct or obtain a three-way or "Y" harness adapter with the correct pre-installed connector pins. This type of harness is installed by disconnecting the existing CAN pins from the main wiring harness wherever you have chosen to effect access, and re-installing them into the "Y" harness, thus forking / splitting the CAN signal into a breakout cable to your capture device.
    • "Posi-tap" is far less complicated than the pin breakout method, but requires a special tapping connector that physically pierces the CAN wire to reach the copper inside. Though there are probably over a thousand Porsche owners with taps like this, some users have had bad outcomes accidentally breaking a CAN wire that required dealer repairs.
  • With either method, some wiring experience is required along with a general comfort level in modifying your vehicle. Some race or performance Porsche shops are capable of installing taps and harnesses for you.

Understanding 718 CAN Bus Options & Access Locations

There are six different CAN buses on a 718 serving different endpoints. In addition there are two secondary buses called MOST and LIN that are outside this discussion. These are visualized in the Porsche 718 SIT manual as follows – including all of the devices on each individual CAN bus:

The Drive CAN is the main bus that is accessed for motorsport telemetry, which makes sense when you study what connects to it. However, because the CAN Gateway forwards much (but not all) of the signals between buses it may be possible to get most (but not all) of the same data on the Chassis CAN or the MMI CAN. The master table contains 3 columns indicating which signals are on which CANs based on research done by the contributors to this site. For example, brake pressure, 6MT Gear and boost pressure are all on the Drive CAN but do not appear on the Chassis CAN. However, choice of CAN is most often constrained by vehicle type and installer wiring experience, so you may simply have to make do with Chassis or even MMI CAN if no other access exists.

Bibliography of Great Books on Motorsports Telemetry

Many books have been written on this topic. Here are four well known titles. Most are easy reads without much science or math education required – the books cover all the relevant topics.

  • Making Sense of Squiggly Lines: Chris Brown: 9780983259312: Amazon.com: Books
  • A Practical Guide to Race Car Data Analysis: Knox, Bob: 9781456587918: Amazon.com: Books
  • Analysis Techniques for Racecar Data Acquisition, Second Edition: Segers, Jorge: 9780768064599: Amazon.com: Books
  • Race Car Vehicle Dynamics: Milliken, Douglas & William
